It is important to note that the pilot trial showed no concerns regarding plugging or any other operational issues. Inspection after operation of the reactor and collection components also showed no concern. Therefore, we have high confidence in the execution of a 24- hour continuous run. The milestone metric included the production of at least 1 L of plastic-derived oil products. This metric was easily met during continuous operation, with approximately 2 L of oil and > 6 L of wax product. A mass balance of the pilot run is shown in Figure 3.4. The recovered mass yield of the wax product (collected via SF1 and SF2, shown in Figure 3.3.2) was determined to be 33.1 wt%, while the liquid oil yield (collected SF3 and SF4) was 10.2 wt%. The recovered mass yield of the char was 1.3 wt% of the original post-consumer waste plastic feedstock. Volumetric flow and a microGC were used to determine the non-condensable gas yield to be 36.1 wt%. The total recovered mass was measured at 80.7 wt%. The wax yield is noticeably lower than that observed in lab-scale trials conducted at ISU. This is likely due to product hold-up in the collection system vessels and to additional cracking of the vapors into non-condensable gas under TOD conditions. This is supported by previous lab-scale results with pure HDPE where the wax and non-condensable gas yields were around 60 wt% and 30 wt%, respectively. Further trials on the pilot reactor would allow for optimization of the system and maximization of condensable yields. Analysis of the collected waste materials combined with the capabilities of the selected plastic sorting technology, showed that the plastics prepared for pyrolysis contained nearly no PVC. As a result, the originally planned work to install a scrubber (Milestone 4.3.2) and to develop chloride-removal absorption methods (Milestone 4.3.3) was no longer necessary and these tasks were abandoned. Negligible PVC contamination being observed in post-consumer feedstocks is beneficial for pyrolysis-based technologies as PVC when broken down produces dangerous chlorine gas. Figure 3.3.4. This project also established a quantitatively grounded, theory-driven framework for understanding and predicting the thermal degradation of hydrocarbon-based plastics. By integrating automated reaction network generation (ARNG), first-principles calculations, and systematic comparison to experimental pyrolysis data, the work advanced both mechanistic understanding and predictive capability for plastic pyrolysis and downstream upgrading. A central accomplishment was the benchmarking of ARNG-based simulations against experimentally measured product distributions using n-decanes pyrolysis as a model system. The simulations reproduced the experimentally observed dominance of olefins and paraffins at short residence times (1-5s) while revealing specific deficiencies in secondary chemistry that became more pronounced as residence time increased.
